relationship: God asked to deal mercifully with communal sins
rationale: Psalm 64 says words of lawless deeds overpowered the community and that God will make atonement for its impieties. Psalm 78 asks the saving God to be propitious toward the community's sins. The comparison concerns divine action toward confessed communal wrongdoing.

relationship: Divine care for rain-fed land throughout the year
rationale: The psalm says God will bless the year's crown of kindness and that His plains will be rich. Deuteronomy describes hills and plains drinking heaven's rain under God's care from the year's beginning to its end. Both connect annual divine care with the land's fertility.

relationship: Payment of vows within God's house
rationale: The speaker intends to enter God's house and pay vows. Psalm 115 likewise locates intended payment of vows to the Lord in the house's courts before the people. The vow and sanctuary setting are both explicit.

relationship: Wrongdoing and the refusal of prayer
rationale: The psalm asks that the Lord not hear if the speaker was regarding injustice in the heart. Isaiah refuses multiplied supplication from blood-filled hands and commands removal of evil and pursuit of justice. The parallel preserves the psalm's condition rather than declaring it a confession of actual injustice.

Psalm 67 says the Lord will give an utterance to those announcing good news. Isaiah describes the good-news messenger and God's making salvation heard. Both connect good-news proclamation with a divinely supplied utterance or announcement.

relationship: The mountain of God's dwelling and an enduring residence
rationale: Psalm 67 questions the curdled mountains about the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell, then affirms that the Lord will dwell to the end. Psalm 131 explicitly says God chose Zion for His enduring dwelling and rest. The comparison preserves the source's question and does not resolve its unnamed mountain's identity.

relationship: Women with tambourines accompany victory praise
rationale: The psalm's procession includes young women beating tambourines. Exodus describes Miriam and women with timbrels and dances, leading praise after the sea deliverance. This is a specific musical comparison, not an identification of the psalm's procession with Miriam's occasion.

relationship: Egypt and Ethiopia in scenes of approach toward God
rationale: Psalm 67 names Egyptian envoys and Ethiopia hastening its hand toward God. Isaiah places Egypt's labor, Ethiopians' trade and Seboin in a promise ending with acknowledgment of Israel's God. The named nations and divine destination correspond; the differing agents and Isaiah's bondage imagery are not equated with the envoys.

relationship: Adversaries add injury after God has acted
rationale: Psalm 68 accuses opponents of persecuting the one God struck and adding pain to His wounded. Zechariah condemns nations that joined in attack to bring evils when God was a little angry. Both distinguish God's preceding action or anger from the adversaries' additional assault.

relationship: Earth, watery depths and creeping creatures summoned to praise
rationale: Psalm 68 calls the heavens, earth, sea and everything creeping in them to praise. Psalm 148 calls the earth, deeps and creeping things into its creation-wide praise. The sea/deeps and creature groups form the particular comparison.

relationship: Divine distance and the plea for help
rationale: Both combine a request against divine distance with a call to attend to help or support. The paired distance-and-attending clauses supply the correspondence.

Psalm 70 asks for shame for slanderers and for evil-seekers to wrap themselves in shame and confusion. Psalm 108 asks that slanderers wear humiliation and wrap shame like a double cloak. Both picture hostile people covered by shame, while the source's two clauses remain distinct.

relationship: Divine mighty acts announced to the coming generation
rationale: Psalm 70 asks not to be forsaken until God's arm and power are announced to the coming generation. Psalm 77 describes transmission of His mighty acts to children yet to be born so they will hope in Him. The intergenerational purpose is explicit in both; the source's righteousness clause continues into the following unit.

relationship: The whole earth filled with the Lord's glory
rationale: Psalm 71 declares that the whole earth will be filled with God's glory and closes with May it be. Numbers states in the Lord's oath that His glory shall fill all the earth. The same worldwide filling by glory occurs in a doxology and in divine speech.
